title: Disentangling topological and anomalous Hall contributions of skyrmions using Kerr microscopy and thermal transport measurements
authors: H. Heyen, M. Vogel, F. Gossing, J. Walowski, K. Dahmen, J. McCord, M. Münzenberg
abstract: The topological Hall effect is a valuable tool to indicate the presence of topologically protected magnetic structures. In this work, we present topological Hall effect measurements originating from topologically protected skyrmions in Ta/CoFeB/MgO single-layer thick films with a one nanometer thick magnetic layer. The simultaneous occurrence of the small topological Hall effect and the dominating anomalous Hall effect in this material system makes direct detection challenging as compared to bulk or multilayer systems. In electronic transport measurements, both effects' contributions impact electron trajectories in the same way, overlapping in the measurement signal, and require disentanglement. Magneto-optical Kerr microscopy was used to image the surface magnetization, enabling the separation of the topological Hall effect from other Hall effect contributions. These measurements reveal a topological Hall resistivity of $249(18)\,$\si{\pico\ohm\meter} for Ta/CoFeB/MgO layer stacks at room temperature. Magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurements also allow tracking skyrmion formation during external magnetic field sweeps to confirm their occurrence when measuring the topological Hall effect. We verify this outcome by comparing the results with thermal and electrical transport measurements from which we calculate the overall topological quantity that gives rise to the topological Nernst and Hall effect, respectively.
summary: This work addresses the challenge of isolating the subtle topological Hall effect originating from skyrmions within thin magnetic films where it is masked by a dominant anomalous contribution. By combining magneto-optical imaging with both electrical and thermal transport measurements, the authors successfully quantify the characteristic topological response ($ho_{THE}$), providing strong evidence for topologically protected spin textures in these nanoscale systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is separating the small topological Hall effect (THE) signal from the much larger, overlapping anomalous Hall effect (AHE) when measuring skyrmion-related transport phenomena.
main_result: The authors successfully measured a finite topological Hall resistivity of $249(18)\, 	ext{p}\Omega	ext{ m}$ at room temperature and confirmed the existence of topologically protected skyrmions using multiple independent measurements.
method: A combination of Magneto-optical Kerr microscopy (MOKE) to image magnetization, electrical transport measurements for THE, and thermal transport measurements for the Topological Nernst Effect (TNE) were employed.
model_or_system: The study investigates single-layer thick films of Ta/CoFeB/MgO that host topologically protected skyrmion spin structures. The analysis models the total measured resistivity ($ho_{Hall}$) and Nernst effect ($N_{xy}$) as sums of Ordinary, Anomalous, and Topological contributions.
key_observables: Topological Hall resistivity ($ho_{THE}$), Topological Nernst coefficient ($N_{TNE}$), surface magnetization images (MOKE), and coercive field decay parameters.
important_parameters: Room temperature measurements; film thicknesses in the nanometer range; magnetic anisotropy controlling skyrmion stability.
main_assumptions: The topological contribution can be isolated by modeling the total signal as a sum of components, and that comparison between THE and TNE provides robust confirmation of topology despite domain wall scattering effects.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate how AHE and THE hysteresis loops can be separated; one figure shows the setup for measuring THE via electron deflection in a Hall cross configuration.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the difficulty of separating THE from AHE, then detailing the use of MOKE to confirm skyrmion presence. It rigorously disentangles contributions using both electrical (Hall) and thermal (Nernst) transport measurements, culminating in a quantitative measurement of $ho_{THE}$ and $N_{TNE}$.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the rigorous separation of emergent topological responses from conventional extrinsic effects (like AHE) using multiple complementary physical probes (electrical vs. thermal) is highly relevant to understanding complex many-body dynamics in engineered quantum materials.

In Hall effect measurements of (b), the THE signal is hidden at the hysteresis loop edges, where skyrmions get nucleated and becomes clearly visible for higher THE peaks like in (d) or barely visible if it only gets shifted to a different region of the hysteresis loop like in (f).
